synopsis: Validation must finish in less than four months after prototype hardware and software arrive in mid-2027, against a historical baseline of three to four years of physical testing and tuning per machine model [f3, f281, f2029, f1174, f5858]. The research found no case in any industry of a new automatic braking function reaching accepted validation about four months after first representative hardware; vendor claims of sub-day validation concern incremental on-road builds on an existing platform, not that milestone [f58, f1201, f1209, f1211]. The manufacturer has not previously used simulation for this kind of validation, and expert opinion considers a working evidence factory—not completed off-road collision mitigation validation—realistic by mid-2027 [f7512, f10387, f372]. Standards recognize simulation among verification methods and, in ISO 13849-2:2012, among validation methods, but neither passing ISO 3450 nor using example stopping-distance calculations establishes that the complete braking function works [f9456, f9457, f9458, f2361, f7729]. Credible validation requires independently established ground truth with controlled measurement uncertainty, validation of sensor stimulation equipment, and evidence matched to the sensor interface actually consumed by the function; credibility communities have not agreed on validation metrics [f5196, f7473, f4864, f4869, f9357]. Planning must also account for uncertain ISO 19014 revisions expected in October 2026 and baseline the editions actually published at design-verification freeze, while public evidence remains incomplete for manufacturer validation methods, ultrasonic material fidelity, and realistic operator responses [f2330, f2331, f11394, f3944, f3469].
